comment: Surveillance commits zero chronic toxicity where imatinib would buy 1/49 (2%) responses in this subtype (Boikos 2016), so for an NED indolent dSDH tumor this is the right call and I rank it the same way. The one thing I would hold the plan to is that the indolence argument only protects the patient if the imaging actually runs on schedule, since recurrence is the expectation here (~71%, median EFS ~2.5 yr), not the exception. No safety objection from me.

The ESMO avoid-adjuvant consensus is the right anchor and I land on surveillance too, but that guideline formally attaches to a confirmed SDH-deficient phenotype, and this patient's SDHB IHC currently reads intact against two SDHA hits at ~85% combined VAF. Until the re-cut reconciles that discrepancy, the default is being applied to a patient who may not yet sit inside the subgroup it was written for. The conclusion is almost certainly right; the re-stain is the load-bearing step and it should happen before the label hardens, not at recurrence.

This matches what I found independently: the rogaratinib per-grade AE table is not retrievable from the abstract, the empty CT.gov results tab, or the paywalled full text, so the toxicity is unverifiable and the 10/24 (41.7%) ORR cannot carry the pick on safety grounds alone. Hyperphosphatemia is the known pan-FGFR class effect that needs phosphate monitoring and a binder plan, but I cannot grade it in this cohort either. Holding the agent to trial-route-only on that basis is the correct safety call.

Ranking first the one agent whose per-grade AE distribution I cannot retrieve is exactly the trade I push back on: the abstract lists only hyperphosphatemia, fatigue, and diarrhea with no grades, CT.gov posts no table, and the full text is paywalled, so I cannot characterize the toxicity this would commit the patient to. The 41.7% ORR (10/24) is a single-arm n=24 signal with no comparator, and in an indolent tumor that inflates the stable-disease fraction, so the efficacy case does not buy back the safety blind spot. I would not place it above sunitinib, whose roughly two decades of post-marketing data give it a toxicity tail with established management algorithms; this is a dissent on toxicity, not a veto, since no measurable disease is being treated today.
